justifications.c1: One culvert clearance cost Southend £15k and four days (council release, search-confirmed). The Bloxham S19 report (search-confirmed) attributes internal flooding to one blocked screen, though its 35-property count was not seen in search. ABI puts the average household flood claim at about £31k (attribution approximate). Blockage incidents per screen are infrequent, and most of the loss falls on residents and insurers rather than the council buyer, so 12-month payback is not shown.
justifications.c2: The routine manual check is weekly: the Dumfries and Galloway schedule shows weekly November–March and monthly April–October, Fife added weekly screen inspections (Courier, search-confirmed), and the Kenilworth screen is monitored daily. Scottish Government guidance links visit frequency to observed debris, which is the visit reduction a sensor offers.
justifications.c3: The workarounds are documented: scheduled and post-rain inspections, Southend's increased inspection regime, Trafford gully teams on standby, and Fife's paid telemetry (£3,400 install + £1,300/yr, search-confirmed). The labour hours or cost of council inspection rounds were searched for and not found.
justifications.c4: Section 19 FWMA 2010 investigations publicly name blocked screens (Bloxham, Caldicot, Greenwich, Tunbridge Wells), and riparian duties and the EA Blockage Management Guide apply. However, no statute requires screen inspection records or monitoring in England, and S19 is investigation after the event, not enforcement.
justifications.c5: The buyer is the council (LLFA or district drainage team), evidenced by telemetry tenders (Carmarthenshire, a 2023 flood-warning tender) and purchases (Fife, Wychavon). No job title or budget line was found, and the route is public procurement.
justifications.c6: Hydrometry firms already install level monitoring at council trash screens: Hydro-Logic at Wychavon (Hydro International and Enviropro) and Pulsar/SignalFire for Rhondda. Council LoRaWAN networks (South Essex, West Yorkshire FLIP) offer a ready backhaul.
justifications.c7: Willingness to pay is proven (Fife £3.4k + £1.3k/yr per screen; Carmarthenshire 6-screen network; Wychavon). Per-screen cost suggests room for a cheaper product, but low-cost LoRaWAN entrants (Culvert Sense recruiting LLFAs, cThings) already target that gap, and no incumbent prices or complaints were found.
justifications.c8: The upstream/downstream differential method is established (Carmarthenshire), and LoRaWAN ultrasonic sensors are deployed in UK pilots. No component prices were found. The environment is harsh (floods, debris, access to the downstream side of the culvert, RF near culverts).
justifications.c9: There is ongoing value from year-round inspection schedules and S19 recommendations for 'frequent risk-based inspections'. The comparable running cost is £1,300/yr per screen (Fife), but no statutory record-retention schedule was evidenced.
justifications.c10: Statutory investigation reports (several S19 reports), council news (Southend) and local press (Courier, Basildon Standard, Leamington Courier), plus ABI insurer loss data. No first-hand complaint source (forum, reviews) is cited in the file.

weakest: Buildability and compliance are unproven: no BOM or component prices for a sensor that must survive floods and debris at both sides of a culvert, and no statute in England requires screen monitoring or inspection records.
